map.An Axiom City episode — Lessons 6-1 & 6-: An Axiom City episode. Lessons 6-1 & 6-2 in one sitting, with three reader gates. Solve the math to move the story.
map.Pattern distortion below the library, cr: Pattern distortion below the library, crew. It is small, teal, and very rude.
map.Previously: on a rained-out field day, t: Last time: on a rained-out field day, the crew woke VEX, a piece of Ada Vex's Pattern Engine. Since then, the city's signs have been melting into scribbles. Last night, the trail of nonsense led straight to Vexhall Library.
map.Vexhall Library, after closing. The reci: Vexhall Library, after closing. The recipe-card archive, with every fix-it formula in Axiom City, is… confetti.
map.It shredded every recipe card into fract: It tore every recipe card into fraction pieces. Half a card here, a quarter of a card there…
map.Distortion source: Ada's cipher vault, u: Distortion source: Ada's cipher vault, under this floor. Its first ring opens only to correct quotients, the answers to division. Bring tape. Bring brains.
map.Repair plan. This spool holds 3 metres o: The plan: this spool holds 3 metres of archive ribbon. Every patched bundle of card pieces needs a strip exactly one quarter of a metre long.
So the door is really asking 3 ÷ 1/4. How many quarter-metre strips are inside three whole metres? A classic vault.
map.Definitions loaded: the piece-size you d: Words loaded: the piece-size you divide BY is the divisor. The answer you get from division is the quotient. Draw a bar for each metre. Slice each metre into quarter-metre pieces. Count the pieces. Bars do not lie.
map.Dividing by a fraction asks: how many of: Dividing by a fraction asks: how many of that piece fit inside? When the divisor is smaller than 1, more than one piece fits in each whole. So the quotient can be bigger than the number you started with.
map.Reader — you're our fifth crew member. S: Reader, you are our fifth crew member. Set the first notch: slice the ribbon, then split the paste!
Andre's repair ribbon is 3 metres long. Each patched card bundle needs a strip exactly 1/4 metre long. Slice the bar model. How many strips can the crew cut? Then split the paste below.
map.Conceptual: dividing by a fraction asks: Conceptual: dividing by a fraction asks how many of that piece FIT INSIDE the whole amount. The divisor (1/4 metre) is smaller than one metre. So each metre of ribbon holds more than one strip.
map.Procedural: use the bar model. Slice ONE: Procedural: use the bar model. Slice ONE metre into quarter-metre strips and count them. Keep counting metre by metre across all three. For the paste: sharing 2/3 of a jar equally among 4 benches means each bench gets one fourth OF the shaded two-thirds. Slice those shaded parts into four equal rows and read one row.
map.2¼ is a mixed number — a whole number an: 2¼ is a mixed number: a whole number and a fraction stuck together. Write it as one fraction and it is not scary.
map.Shortcut loaded: to divide by a fraction: Shortcut loaded: to divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal, the flipped fraction. ÷ ¾ becomes × 4/3, because ¾ × 4/3 = 1. Flip the divisor, never the starting amount.
map.Two roads, one quotient: count the piece: Two roads, one quotient: count the pieces in a bar model, or flip the divisor and multiply by the reciprocal. Both must agree. That is your built-in error alarm.
map.The restored card: the jar holds 2¼ cups: The restored card: the jar holds 2¼ cups of glow-paste and one batch uses ¾ cup. Lock A: how many batches can the crew mix? Lock B: Mateo's copper tape is 1½ metres. Each card spine needs ¼ metre. How many spines can he tape?
map.Conceptual: a mixed number is a whole nu: Conceptual: a mixed number is a whole number plus a fraction stuck together. Write it as ONE fraction before dividing. And dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal, the flipped fraction.
map.Procedural: make the pieces match. Turn: Procedural: make the pieces match. Turn 2¼ cups into quarter-cups and ¾ cup into quarter-cups. Then count how many batch-sized groups fit. For the tape, dividing by ¼ is multiplying by 4/1, the reciprocal of 1/4.
map.The ring clicks again. The glitch panics: The ring clicks again. The glitch panics and starts scribbling on the vault wall.
map.The divisor's size decides everything. D: The divisor's size decides everything. Divide by a number bigger than 1 → the quotient gets smaller. Divide by a fraction smaller than 1 → the quotient grows. The glitch is betting you won't check.
map.VEX projects a demo board on the vault d: VEX shows a demo board on the vault door. Time to get ready to fight back.
map.So every answer carries its own receipt:: So every answer comes with its own receipt: multiply the quotient by the divisor and you must land back on the start.
map.Always run the receipt: quotient × divis: Always run the receipt: quotient × divisor = the amount you started with. If it doesn't, the division is wrong, no matter how sure the glitch sounds.
map.The inner ring. Three locks. The glitch: The inner ring. Three locks. The glitch puffs up to twice its size, still quite small.
Reader, three locks, one lying glitch. Do the divisions. Then find the counterexample that breaks its lie in half.
map.Boss Gate ahead: two quotients to comput: Boss Gate ahead: two quotients to find, one lie to break with a single counterexample.
map.BOSS GATE. Three locks. One lying glitch: BOSS GATE. Three locks. One lying glitch. (You can do this. Probably. Yes.)
map.Conceptual: the divisor's size decides t: Conceptual: the divisor's size decides what happens to the quotient. Dividing by a fraction SMALLER than 1 makes the quotient BIGGER than the start, because small pieces fit many times. Dividing by a number bigger than 1 shrinks it.
map.Procedural: flip each divisor into its r: Procedural: flip each divisor into its reciprocal and multiply: ÷ 2/5 becomes × 5/2. For ÷ 1¼, write 1¼ as 5/4 first, then × 4/5. For the lie-lock, look for a division whose quotient is BIGGER than the number it started with.
map.The ring split it into harmless sparks!: The ring broke it into harmless sparks! And look, the cards are taping THEMSELVES back together.
map.Quotients verified. First ring: open. Li: Quotients checked. First ring: open. Library signs: fixing their own spelling as we speak.
map.One ring down. But the sparks flew DEEPE: One ring down. But the sparks flew DEEPER into the vault, toward a door covered in tiny raised numbers…
map.Quotient & divisor.The divisor is the pi: Quotient & divisor.The divisor is the piece-size you divide by. The quotient is the answer. "3 ÷ 1/4" asks how many quarter-metre strips fit inside 3 metres. A bar model shows every piece.
map.Mixed numbers & the reciprocal.Rewrite a: Mixed numbers & the reciprocal.Write a mixed number as one fraction. Then divide by multiplying by the divisor's reciprocal, the flipped fraction. ÷ ¾ becomes × 4/3.
map.completed Unit 6 · Episode 1: Split the: finished Unit 6 · Episode 1: Split the Glitch and showed mastery of dividing fractions and mixed numbers.
map.Different shelf, same idea: Ms. Ortiz's: New shelf, same idea: Ms. Ortiz's twine is 6 metres, and each label tag needs a 1/3-metre piece. Ask it as a fit question: how many 1/3s fit inside 6?
map.Bar model: draw 6 one-metre bars. Slice: Bar model: draw 6 one-metre bars. Slice each metre into thirds. Every metre holds 3 third-metre pieces.
map.Count all the pieces: 6 metres × 3 piece: Count all the pieces: 6 metres × 3 pieces per metre = 18 pieces. Receipt: 18 × 1/3 = 6. The quotient times the divisor gives back the start.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.Different card, same moves: 1¾ cups of s: New card, same moves: 1¾ cups of syrup, and each glaze uses ½ cup. Write the mixed number first: 1¾ = 7/4.
map.Sense check: three whole glazes and half: Sense check: three whole glazes and half of another. Receipt: 3½ × ½ = 1¾. It gives back the start, so the quotient is good.
map.Demo lock: 2 jars of ink, and each stamp: Demo lock: 2 jars of ink, and each stamp pad uses 2/5 of a jar. Flip the divisor: 2 ÷ 2/5 = 2 × 5/2.
map.Receipt: 5 × 2/5 = 2. Quotient × divisor: Receipt: 5 × 2/5 = 2. Quotient × divisor = the start, every time, even when the quotient grew.
map.Type a strip count first — the bar model: Type a strip count first. The bar model will shade as you go.
map.That's 3/4 of a METRE — you took one qua: That is 3/4 of a METRE. You took one quarter OF the ribbon instead. The lock asks how many quarter-metre strips FIT INSIDE 3 metres. Count the small boxes.
map.The ring buzzes. Shade the bar model: ho: The ring buzzes. Shade the bar model: how many quarter-metre boxes fill ONE metre? Keep counting across all three metres.
map.Ribbon sliced! Now split the paste — pic: Ribbon sliced! Now split the paste. Pick how much each bench gets.
map.6 jars?! Sharing among 4 benches can't g: 6 jars?! Sharing among 4 benches cannot give each bench MORE paste than there is. Sharing splits the amount, so each share is smaller than 2/3.
map.8/3 jars means you MULTIPLIED by 4. Shar: 8/3 jars means you MULTIPLIED by 4. Sharing among 4 benches means dividing: each bench gets one fourth OF the 2/3 jar.
map.So close — that's one fourth of one THIR: So close. That is one fourth of one THIRD. The benches share two thirds. Slice both shaded thirds into 4 rows and count what one row holds.
map.Lock 1 turns! 12 quarter-metre strips fi: Lock 1 turns! 12 quarter-metre strips fit in 3 metres (12 × 1/4 m = 3 m), and 2/3 ÷ 4 = 1/6 of a jar per bench. The first notch clicks into place.
map.The card waits. Fill in both locks — bat: The card waits. Fill in both locks. Batches first, then spines.
map.Lock A jams — that's 2¼ × ¾. You multipl: Lock A jams. That is 2¼ × ¾. You multiplied BY the divisor. To divide by ¾, flip it and multiply by 4/3 instead.
map.Lock A holds. Rewrite 2¼ as one fraction: Lock A holds. Write 2¼ as one fraction made of quarters. Then ask how many ¾-cup groups fit inside it. Or flip ¾ and multiply.
map.Lock B jams — that's 1½ × ¼. Don't shrin: Lock B jams. That is 1½ × ¼. Don't shrink the tape! Dividing by ¼ asks how many quarter-metres FIT, so multiply by the reciprocal, 4/1.
map.Lock B holds. 1½ is a mixed number — rew: Lock B holds. 1½ is a mixed number. Write it as halves or quarters first. Then count quarter-metre pieces, or multiply by 4.
map.Lock 1 jams — that's 4 × 2/5. You multip: Lock 1 jams. That is 4 × 2/5. You multiplied by the divisor. Flip it: dividing by 2/5 means multiplying by 5/2.
map.Lock 1 holds. Each jar holds two and a h: Lock 1 holds. Each jar holds two and a half servings of 2/5. Or just flip the divisor: 4 × 5/2.
map.Lock 2 jams — that's 3¾ × 1¼. Don't mult: Lock 2 jams. That is 3¾ × 1¼. Don't multiply the board by the divisor. Write both mixed numbers as quarters, then divide.
map.Lock 2 holds. Rewrite 3¾ and 1¼ as quart: Lock 2 holds. Write 3¾ and 1¼ as quarters so the pieces match. Then count how many drawer-front lengths fit.
map.Lock 3 holds. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 SHRANK — that r: Lock 3 holds. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 got SMALLER. That feeds the lie instead of breaking it. Find a division whose answer GREW.
map.Lock 3 holds. 4 × 2/5 is a MULTIPLICATIO: Lock 3 holds. 4 × 2/5 is a MULTIPLICATION. The lie is about dividing. Beat it with a division.
map.Lock 3 holds. 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 is true, but 3: Lock 3 holds. 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 is true, but 3 is SMALLER than 3¾. The glitch just smirks. Pick the quotient that ended up bigger than its start.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 scorches, 3: ALL LOCKS OPEN. 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 scorches, 3¾ ÷ 1¼ = 3 drawer fronts. And 4 ÷ 2/5 = 10 is the counterexample: the quotient GREW, so dividing does not always shrink. The lie snaps, the ring spins, and the glitch breaks into harmless sparks!
Yes! Now go back and open that gate.
map.Walk the steps above again — you've got: Go over the steps above again. You can do this.
